description: Master the fundamentals of HTTP communication and learn to use Python's requests library.

slides.title: Introduction to HTTP
slides.content:
# The Language of the Web 🌐

HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the foundation of data communication on the World Wide Web.

When you visit a website or scrape data, your Python code acts as a **Client**. It sends an HTTP **Request** to a **Server**, and the server responds with an HTTP **Response** (usually containing HTML or JSON data).

If you want to extract data from the internet, you MUST understand how HTTP works.

slides.title: HTTP Methods
slides.content:
# HTTP Methods (Verbs) 🗣️

When making a request, you must specify the *Method*. This tells the server what action you want to perform.

- **GET:** Retrieve data from the server. (e.g., viewing a webpage, fetching API data).
- **POST:** Send data to the server to create a new resource. (e.g., submitting a login form, uploading a file).
- **PUT / PATCH:** Update an existing resource on the server.
- **DELETE:** Remove a resource from the server.

For Web Scraping, you will use **GET** 90% of the time, and **POST** when trying to bypass login forms.

slides.title: The Requests Library
slides.content:
# Python's Requests Library 🐍

The `requests` library is the de facto standard for making HTTP requests in Python. It is incredibly user-friendly.

## Installation
```bash
pip install requests
```

## Making a GET Request
```python_not
import requests

# Fetch data from a URL
response = requests.get('https://api.github.com')

# Did it succeed?
print(response.status_code) # 200 means OK!
```

slides.title: HTTP Status Codes
slides.content:
# Status Codes 🚦

Every HTTP response comes with a 3-digit status code telling you what happened.

- **1xx (Informational):** Request received.
- **2xx (Success):** Action successfully received, understood, and accepted. (e.g., **200 OK**, 201 Created).
- **3xx (Redirection):** Further action must be taken to complete the request. (e.g., **301 Moved Permanently**).
- **4xx (Client Error):** The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled. (e.g., **404 Not Found**, **401 Unauthorized**, **403 Forbidden**).
- **5xx (Server Error):** The server failed to fulfill a valid request. (e.g., **500 Internal Server Error**).

slides.title: Inspecting the Response
slides.content:
# Reading the Data 📖

Once you have a `response` object, how do you read the data?

```python_not
import requests
response = requests.get('https://api.github.com')

# To get the raw text (HTML string)
print(response.text)

# To get the raw bytes (useful for downloading images/files)
print(response.content)

# If the server returns JSON, requests can parse it directly into a Python Dictionary!
data = response.json()
print(data['current_user_url'])
```

slides.title: Query Parameters
slides.content:
# Query Parameters 🔍

Often, you need to send data in the URL itself (e.g., `https://example.com/search?q=python&page=2`).

Instead of concatenating strings, `requests` lets you pass a dictionary!

```python_not
payload = {'q': 'python', 'page': 2}
response = requests.get('https://example.com/search', params=payload)

# Check the URL that was actually constructed
print(response.url)
```
This handles URL encoding (converting spaces to `%20`) automatically.

slides.title: HTTP Headers
slides.content:
# HTTP Headers 🎩

Headers are hidden key-value pairs sent with every request and response. They contain metadata about the browser, the data format, authorization, etc.

## The User-Agent
The most important header for scraping is the `User-Agent`. It tells the server what browser you are using.
By default, Python's requests library sends `python-requests/2.x.x`.

**Many servers block default Python requests!** You must fake it:

```python_not
headers = {
    'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/91.0.4472.124 Safari/537.36'
}
response = requests.get('https://example.com', headers=headers)
```

slides.title: POST Requests and Forms
slides.content:
# Submitting Forms 📝

To simulate a user submitting a form (like a login), you make a POST request and pass a `data` dictionary.

```python_not
login_data = {
    'username': 'my_user',
    'password': 'secret_password'
}

response = requests.post('https://example.com/login', data=login_data)

if "Welcome back" in response.text:
    print("Login successful!")
```

slides.title: Cookies
slides.content:
# Cookies 🍪

HTTP is a *stateless* protocol. Every request is completely independent. 
How does a website remember you are logged in when you click a new page? **Cookies.**

Cookies are small pieces of data the server sends in the response, which your browser saves and sends back on subsequent requests.

```python_not
# Reading cookies from a response
response = requests.get('https://google.com')
print(response.cookies['1P_JAR'])

# Sending cookies with a request
my_cookies = {'session_id': 'xyz123'}
requests.get('https://example.com/dashboard', cookies=my_cookies)
```

slides.title: Sessions
slides.content:
# Session Objects 🛒

Manually passing cookies back and forth is annoying. 
A `Session` object does this for you automatically! It persists cookies across all requests made from the Session instance.

```python_not
session = requests.Session()

# 1. Log in (Server sends a session cookie)
session.post('https://example.com/login', data={'user': 'me', 'pass': '123'})

# 2. Visit a protected page (Session automatically sends the cookie!)
response = session.get('https://example.com/protected_dashboard')
print(response.text)
```
This is essential for scraping websites behind a login wall!

slides.title: Authentication (OAuth & Tokens)
slides.content:
# API Authentication 🔐

Many APIs require authentication. Instead of a username/password form, they use tokens.

## Bearer Tokens
A common pattern is sending a token in the `Authorization` header.

```python_not
headers = {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_SECRET_API_TOKEN'
}
response = requests.get('https://api.example.com/v1/data', headers=headers)
```

## Basic Auth
Some older APIs use HTTP Basic Auth. `requests` has a built-in parameter for this:
```python_not
from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth
response = requests.get('https://api.example.com', auth=HTTPBasicAuth('user', 'pass'))
```

slides.title: Pagination
slides.content:
# Handling Pagination 📚

APIs rarely return all their data at once. They return it in "pages" to save bandwidth.
To get all data, you must write a loop.

```python_not
all_data = []
page = 1

while True:
    response = requests.get(f'https://api.example.com/items?page={page}')
    data = response.json()
    
    if not data['items']: 
        break # We hit an empty page, stop looping!
        
    all_data.extend(data['items'])
    page += 1

print(f"Fetched {len(all_data)} total items.")
```

slides.title: Rate Limiting
slides.content:
# Rate Limiting & Throttling 🛑

If you make 1000 requests per second, a server might think you are a DDoS attack and ban your IP address.
APIs enforce **Rate Limits** (e.g., 60 requests per minute).

If you exceed it, the server usually returns a **429 Too Many Requests** status code.

## Be Polite!
Always respect rate limits and `time.sleep()` in your scraping loops.
```python_not
import time
import requests

for url in list_of_urls:
    response = requests.get(url)
    # ... process data ...
    time.sleep(1) # Wait 1 second before the next request
```

slides.title: Handling Exceptions
slides.content:
# Defensive Scraping 🛡️

Networks are unreliable. Servers crash. APIs change. Your code must handle exceptions.

```python_not
try:
    # timeout=5 ensures the request gives up after 5 seconds of hanging
    response = requests.get('https://example.com', timeout=5)
    
    # Raises an exception if status code is 4xx or 5xx
    response.raise_for_status() 
    
except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as errh:
    print ("HTTP Error:",errh)
except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError as errc:
    print ("Error Connecting:",errc)
except requests.exceptions.Timeout as errt:
    print ("Timeout Error:",errt)
```

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Summary 🎉

You are now ready to communicate with the World Wide Web using Python!

## Key Takeaways
- ✅ **HTTP Methods:** Use GET to fetch data, and POST to submit data.
- ✅ **Status Codes:** 200 is good, 404 is missing, 500 is a server crash, 429 is rate-limited.
- ✅ **Requests Library:** Python's best tool for making HTTP requests.
- ✅ **Headers:** Use the `User-Agent` header to disguise your script as a real browser to prevent getting blocked.
- ✅ **Sessions:** Use `requests.Session()` to automatically save and send cookies across requests (crucial for logins).
- ✅ **Pagination & Rate Limits:** Always use loops to fetch multi-page data, and `time.sleep()` to avoid getting banned.
